questions.question: What is the Backend for Frontend (BFF) pattern?

options.text: A dedicated backend service tailored for each frontend type (web, mobile, etc.)

questions.explanation: BFF: separate backend per frontend. Web BFF, iOS BFF, Android BFF. Each optimized for its client's needs. Coined by Sam Newman. Solves: one-size-fits-all API problem.

questions.question: What problem does BFF solve?

options.text: Different frontends have different data needs—BFF provides tailored APIs for each

questions.explanation: Problem: mobile needs minimal data (bandwidth), web needs rich data, TV needs different format. Generic API = over-fetching or under-fetching. BFF: each frontend gets exactly what it needs.

questions.question: How does BFF differ from API Gateway?

options.text: API Gateway routes requests; BFF contains client-specific business logic and data aggregation

questions.explanation: API Gateway: routing, auth, rate limiting—generic concerns. BFF: client-specific logic, data transformation, aggregation tailored to frontend needs. BFF sits behind gateway or replaces it for specific clients.

questions.question: Who typically owns a BFF service?

options.text: The frontend team that consumes it

questions.explanation: BFF ownership: frontend team owns their BFF. They know their needs best. Reduces coordination overhead. Frontend team can evolve BFF without backend team bottleneck. Enables autonomy.

questions.question: What is a common anti-pattern when implementing BFF?

options.text: Putting too much business logic in BFF instead of keeping it in domain services

questions.explanation: Anti-pattern: BFF becomes 'smart' with business logic. Should be: thin translation layer. Business logic belongs in domain services. BFF: aggregate, transform, adapt—not compute business rules.

questions.question: How does BFF help with mobile app performance?

options.text: Reduces payload size, minimizes round trips, and optimizes for mobile constraints

questions.explanation: Mobile BFF optimizations: smaller payloads (mobile bandwidth), fewer round trips (latency), compressed responses, offline-friendly data structures, battery-conscious polling strategies. Tailored for mobile constraints.

questions.question: What is the trade-off of having multiple BFFs?

options.text: Code duplication across BFFs and increased operational complexity

questions.explanation: BFF trade-offs: code duplication (similar logic in each BFF), more services to deploy/monitor, potential inconsistency between clients. Mitigation: shared libraries, clear boundaries, good documentation.

questions.question: When should you NOT use BFF?

options.text: When you have only one client type or clients have very similar needs

questions.explanation: Skip BFF when: single client type, similar client needs, small team (overhead not worth it), simple API requirements. BFF adds complexity—only use when client diversity justifies it.

questions.question: How does BFF handle authentication?

options.text: Each BFF has its own auth system
BFF validates tokens and may transform auth context for downstream services
Authentication is handled only by frontend

questions.explanation: BFF auth: validates JWT/session from client, extracts user context, passes to downstream services (often as internal token or headers). May handle client-specific auth flows (OAuth for web, biometric for mobile).

questions.question: What is GraphQL's relationship to BFF?

options.text: GraphQL can serve as a BFF, allowing clients to request exactly the data they need

questions.explanation: GraphQL as BFF: clients specify exact data needs. Reduces over/under-fetching. Can replace multiple REST BFFs with single GraphQL endpoint. Trade-off: complexity, caching challenges. Netflix, Airbnb use this approach.

questions.question: How should BFFs communicate with backend services?

options.text: Through well-defined service APIs, not bypassing service boundaries

questions.explanation: BFF communication: call backend service APIs. Never bypass to databases directly. Maintains service encapsulation. Use: REST, gRPC, GraphQL federation. BFF is a client of backend services.

questions.question: Your company has web, iOS, and Android apps with very different data needs. What's the recommended approach?

options.text: Three BFFs—one per platform—each optimized for its client's specific needs

questions.explanation: Three platforms, different needs = three BFFs. Web BFF: rich data, SEO support. iOS/Android BFFs: optimized payloads, offline support. Each team owns their BFF. Shared backend services underneath.
